title: Financial Crime Supervision in the Age of AI
summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors to assess financial crime controls and firms' use of AI in monitoring, screening, fraud and surveillance.
topic: Reducing Financial Crime & Delivering Market Integrity
intro: This training programme equips supervisory staff to assess firms' financial crime controls as AI transforms both detection and criminality: from AML/CFT foundations and sanctions to AI-driven monitoring, fraud and new generative AI typologies.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give supervisors a firm grounding in risk-based AML/CFT, sanctions and market abuse supervision, together with the technical understanding to assess firms' use of AI to detect financial crime. Participants leave able to challenge AI-driven monitoring and screening, recognise emerging AI-enabled typologies and form evidence-based supervisory judgements.
sections.What It Covers: The AML/CFT framework and risk-based approach, ML/TF typologies, supervising AML/CFT controls, AI in transaction monitoring, model risk in financial crime systems, sanctions and adverse media screening, fraud and behavioural analytics, generative AI typologies, market abuse surveillance, and bias, accountability and SupTech.
Intended Audience: AML/CFT, sanctions and financial crime supervisors and inspectors
Market surveillance, conduct and data analytics staff working on financial crime risk
Senior managers shaping the authority's financial crime strategy and use of SupTech
Learning Objectives: Explain the international AML/CFT framework and apply a risk-based supervisory approach
Identify ML/TF, fraud and market abuse typologies and the red flags they leave
Assess how firms use AI and machine learning in monitoring, screening and fraud detection
Evaluate model risk, explainability, bias and human oversight in financial crime AI
Challenge firms' resilience to new typologies enabled by generative AI
Design the authority's supervisory response, including its own use of SupTech
sections.Structure and Format: Ten modules of about three hours each, grouped into three pathways and delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a multi-day programme or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines a technical briefing with case studies, red flags and supervisory question exercises, and pathways or individual modules can be selected or tailored to the authority's needs.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some experience of AML/CFT, sanctions or conduct supervision is helpful. No technical background in AI or data science is required.
Core Reading: FATF, International Standards on Combating Money Laundering and the Financing of Terrorism and Proliferation: The FATF Recommendations (as updated)
FATF, Opportunities and Challenges of New Technologies for AML/CFT (2021)

modules.title: The AML/CFT Framework and Risk-Based Supervision
modules.summary: The international foundations of AML/CFT supervision, the FATF Recommendations and mutual evaluations, and how authorities apply a risk-based approach to their populations of firms.
objectives: Explain the FATF standards and the supervisor's role within the national AML/CFT system
Apply a risk-based approach to supervisory planning and resourcing
Describe how mutual evaluations assess supervisory effectiveness
syllabus: FATF Recommendations, immediate outcomes and mutual evaluations
National risk assessment, sector risk assessment and firm risk scoring
Roles of the supervisor, the national FIU and law enforcement
Regional AML frameworks and the move to supranational supervision

modules.title: ML/TF Typologies and Red Flags
modules.summary: The main money laundering and terrorist financing typologies across banking, payments, investment and digital asset channels, and how to recognise red flags in real cases.
objectives: Identify key ML/TF typologies across sectors and channels
Recognise red flags in customer, transaction and structural data
Determine appropriate escalation when red flags are found
syllabus: Placement, layering and integration in modern financial channels
Trade-based laundering, professional enablers and complex structures
Terrorist and proliferation financing typologies
Case study: tracing red flags through a laundering scheme

modules.title: Supervising AML/CFT Controls in Practice
modules.summary: How to assess a firm's AML/CFT governance, business-wide risk assessment, due diligence and monitoring, and translate findings into consistent supervisory action.
objectives: Assess a firm's AML/CFT governance and business-wide risk assessment
Evaluate customer due diligence, monitoring and suspicious activity reporting
Apply consistent supervisory judgement and follow-up
syllabus: Board oversight, the AML compliance officer and management information
Customer due diligence, enhanced due diligence and beneficial ownership
Desk-based reviews, onsite inspections and sample testing
From findings to remediation plans and enforcement referral

modules.title: AI and Machine Learning in Transaction Monitoring
modules.summary: How firms move from rules-based to AI-driven monitoring using anomaly detection and network analytics, and the detection trade-offs supervisors should expect firms to manage.
objectives: Explain how AI and machine learning techniques are applied to transaction monitoring
Assess claims about false-positive reduction and detection performance
Challenge whether systems are tuned for detection rather than workload
syllabus: Rules-based versus AI-driven monitoring: capabilities and limits
Anomaly detection, behavioural profiling and graph analytics
False positives, false negatives and reading performance metrics critically
Case study: an AI monitoring system under supervisory review

modules.title: Supervising AI-Driven Financial Crime Systems

objectives: Explain model risk as it applies to AI-driven financial crime systems
Describe expectations for model validation and ongoing monitoring
Assess the explainability of an AI-driven financial crime system
Evaluate the governance framework surrounding an AI model's deployment
Formulate a supervisory assessment of an AI-driven financial crime system

Model risk lifecycle: development, validation, deployment, monitoring
Why financial crime AI models pose distinct governance challenges
Regulatory expectations for model risk management

Model validation standards and independent review
Ongoing monitoring for model drift and degradation
Explainability techniques for complex models
Balancing model sophistication against explainability needs
Group exercise: assess a sample model validation report for adequacy
Governance framework expectations: ownership, sign-off, escalation
Case study: a firm's AI model governance under review
Case study: formulate a supervisory assessment of a firm's AI financial crime system
Recap: model risk, validation, explainability, governance
Reflection and discussion
Q&A

Describe the challenges of PEP identification at scale
Assess the calibration of an adverse media monitoring system
Evaluate alert quality and escalation processes
Identify supervisory red flags in a firm's screening framework
syllabus: Fuzzy matching techniques in sanctions list screening
NLP-based approaches to name and entity matching
Challenges of PEP identification: scale, data quality, false matches
Regulatory expectations for sanctions screening effectiveness
Facilitated discussion: sanctions screening challenges from participants' own experience
How adverse media monitoring tools work
Calibrating sensitivity to avoid both under- and over-alerting
Assessing alert quality and escalation workflows
Common calibration failures
Group exercise: assess the calibration of a sample adverse media monitoring configuration
Common red flags in a firm's screening framework
Case study: a screening framework with calibration weaknesses
Case study: identify red flags and propose supervisory follow-up
Recap: fuzzy matching, PEP challenges, calibration, red flags
Reflection and discussion
Q&A

modules.title: Fraud Detection & Behavioural Analytics
modules.summary: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' understanding of how AI-enabled fraud detection systems operate across payments and banking channels, examining behavioural analytics and biometric techniques, and the supervisory considerations for assessing firms' fraud…
objectives: Explain how real-time fraud scoring systems operate
Describe behavioural biometric techniques used in fraud detection
Assess common payment fraud typologies
Evaluate the adequacy of a firm's fraud control framework
Identify supervisory considerations for assessing fraud detection effectiveness
syllabus: How real-time fraud scoring works across payment channels
Data inputs: transaction, device, behavioural signals
Speed versus accuracy trade-offs in real-time decisioning
Regulatory expectations for fraud control frameworks
Facilitated discussion: fraud typologies observed by participants
Behavioural biometric techniques: typing patterns, device handling
Common payment fraud typologies: APP fraud, account takeover, card fraud
Strengths and limitations of biometric fraud detection
Privacy considerations in behavioural biometrics
Group exercise: map fraud typologies to appropriate detection techniques

Case study: a firm's fraud control framework under review
Case study: evaluate a firm's fraud control framework and identify supervisory considerations
Recap: fraud scoring, biometrics, typologies, framework assessment
Reflection and discussion
Q&A

modules.title: Generative AI and Emerging Financial Crime Typologies
modules.summary: How criminals use generative AI for synthetic identities, deepfake onboarding and large-scale social engineering, and the resilience firms and supervisors need to build.
objectives: Recognise financial crime typologies enabled by generative AI
Assess firms' identity verification and liveness controls
Challenge firms' resilience against AI-enabled social engineering
syllabus: Synthetic identity fraud and deepfake-enabled onboarding
Voice cloning, deepfake video and AI-generated phishing
Liveness detection, multi-factor verification and their limits
Case study: a firm targeted by a deepfake-enabled fraud

modules.title: Market Abuse Detection & Surveillance
modules.summary: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' understanding of how market abuse is detected through surveillance systems, and how supervisors assess the adequacy of firms' own surveillance and monitoring capability.
objectives: Explain the main categories of market abuse
Describe how trade surveillance systems detect suspicious trading patterns
Assess cross-market and cross-asset surveillance challenges
Evaluate the adequacy of a firm's surveillance framework
Formulate a supervisory assessment of a market abuse case
syllabus: Insider dealing, market manipulation, and unlawful disclosure
Evolving typologies: spoofing, layering, cross-market manipulation
Why market abuse undermines market integrity and confidence
The supervisor's role in market surveillance

How trade surveillance systems detect suspicious patterns
Alert generation, tuning, and false-positive management
Cross-market and cross-asset surveillance challenges
Data and technology requirements for effective surveillance
Group exercise: review sample surveillance alerts and assess plausibility of abuse
Criteria for assessing a firm's surveillance framework adequacy
Case study: a suspected market abuse case
Case study: formulate a supervisory assessment of a market abuse case
Recap: abuse categories, surveillance systems, framework assessment
Reflection and discussion
Q&A

modules.title: Bias, Accountability and the Authority's Own SupTech
modules.summary: Brings the programme together by examining fairness and accountability in financial crime AI and how the authority can use data and AI in its own supervision.
objectives: Assess bias and discriminatory outcomes in financial crime AI, including de-risking
Evaluate audit trails and human-in-the-loop safeguards
Design priorities for the authority's financial crime SupTech
syllabus: Bias sources, testing methods and remediation options
Audit trails, accountability and customer impact of AI-driven decisions
SupTech for AML/CFT: risk scoring, network analysis and data sharing
Workshop: the authority's financial crime and AI action plan

related.title: Asset Recovery: Tracing, Freezing and Confiscation

related.title: Enforcement and Sanctions
related.summary: A ten-module programme taking enforcement and supervisory staff through the full life of an enforcement case, from triage and evidence to sanctions, settlement and cooperation.

related.title: Financial Investigation: Following the Money
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping investigators and analysts to run parallel financial investigations, trace funds through accounts and corporate vehicles, and present financial evidence.
